result:
Rain has a way of changing the atmosphere of a city. Sidewalks become mirrors, umbrellas bloom in every color, and traffic sounds soften beneath the steady percussion of droplets. Even a familiar street can feel briefly mysterious, as if the rain has folded the ordinary world into a kinder, quieter version of itself.

I like walking during a light shower, especially when the pavement is warm and the air smells of dust, soil, and distant pavement. Puddles gather in cracks and along curbs, holding tiny reflections of shop signs and clouds. Each footstep sends a small crown of water upward. There is something playful about that, a reminder that even the heaviest storms begin with individual drops.

Rain also alters time. A five minute delay can stretch into twenty, and plans dissolve as easily as sugar in a puddle. Yet this inconvenience often produces unexpected rewards: a conversation with someone under a shared umbrella, a forgotten book discovered at a café, a long look at a garden while waiting for the clouds to pass.

Perhaps that is why rain feels restorative. It interrupts our schedules and asks us to notice what we usually overlook. It cools hot pavement, fills dry rivers, and gives tired cities a chance to breathe. After the shower, leaves shine, colors deepen, and the air carries the clean scent of renewal.

I no longer resent rain. I step outside, let drops meet my face, and walk slowly. Sometimes rain is rain; sometimes, an invitation to begin.
